articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's short-term rental crackdown enters year two. Code enforcement still can't keep up.
articles.dek: The county hired two new inspectors and passed stricter rules. Complaints are up 40 percent anyway. A look at why the whack-a-mole continues.
brief: Escambia County received 847 STR-related complaints in the first six months of 2026, up from 604 in the same period last year despite new enforcement staff and stricter ordinances
Two code enforcement officers hired specifically for STR violations have issued 312 citations since January, but the county's legal department has only processed 89 cases to completion
Property owners and management companies have learned to exploit a 30-day cure period in the county code, resetting the enforcement clock by making temporary corrections
articles.body:
The house at 14502 Perdido Key Drive threw a party on Memorial Day weekend. Not a small one. The kind with valet parking on the shoulder of the road and a rented speaker system that rattled windows three lots over.

By 11 p.m., Escambia County's code enforcement hotline had logged four complaints. By 2 a.m., sheriff's deputies had responded twice. By Monday morning, the listing was back up on Airbnb with a fresh five-star review: "Perfect spot for our group getaway!"

The property has been cited three times since October 2025. It remains in operation.

"We're not losing the battle," said Marcus Henderson, director of Escambia County's Development Services Department. "But we're not winning it either."

The numbers tell a familiar story

When the Board of County Commissioners passed its revised short-term rental ordinance in June 2025, the rhetoric was muscular. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh called it "the strongest enforcement mechanism in Northwest Florida." Commissioner May Litchfield predicted complaints would drop by half within a year.

They were wrong.

The county received 847 STR-related complaints between January 1 and June 30, 2026. The same period last year saw 604. That's a 40 percent increase.

Noise complaints account for 38 percent of the total. Parking violations make up another 29 percent. The rest splits among trash, occupancy limits and unpermitted rentals operating without the county's required registration.

The two code enforcement officers hired last August specifically to handle STR violations have been busy. Officer Denise Watkins and Officer Carlos Muniz have together issued 312 citations in six months. That's roughly one per working day, each.

But citations are not conclusions.

The 30-day loophole

Escambia County's code allows property owners 30 days to "cure" a violation before penalties escalate. The intent was reasonable. Give people time to fix a broken fence or trim an overgrown hedge. Don't punish first-time mistakes with maximum fines.

STR operators figured out the exploit almost immediately.

Here's how it works: Code enforcement issues a citation for, say, exceeding the posted occupancy limit of 12 guests. The owner responds within the cure period by submitting documentation—sometimes just a written statement—claiming the violation has been addressed. The clock resets. Thirty days later, the same property hosts 18 people for a bachelorette party. New citation. New cure period. Repeat.

"They're playing the system exactly as the system allows them to," said Watkins in an interview at the code enforcement office on Stefani Road. "I can't cite them for being smart."

Of the 312 citations issued this year, only 89 have been processed to completion by the county attorney's office. Completion means either a fine paid, a case dismissed, or a hearing held before the Code Enforcement Special Magistrate. The other 223 remain in administrative limbo—cure periods extended, appeals filed, documentation pending.

County Attorney Alison Rogers said her office is working through the backlog. "Each case requires review. We can't just rubber-stamp fines. Property owners have due process rights."

She has two attorneys assigned part-time to code enforcement matters. They handle all violations, not just STRs.

Who's actually getting fined

The Special Magistrate has held 34 STR-related hearings since January. Fines have ranged from $150 to $2,500. The median is $500.

For context: A three-bedroom house on Perdido Key rents for $400 to $600 per night during peak season. A single weekend covers most fines.

"The economics don't pencil for compliance," said David Thornton, a real estate attorney in Gulf Breeze who has represented both STR owners and neighbors in disputes. "If I can make $3,000 on a weekend and my worst-case fine is $500, that's just a cost of doing business."

The county's ordinance does allow for escalating penalties—up to $15,000 for repeat offenders and potential revocation of the STR registration. But reaching that threshold requires multiple completed cases against the same property. With the cure period resetting the clock and the legal department backlogged, few properties have accumulated enough finalized violations to trigger maximum penalties.

One has. A property on Via de Luna in Pensacola Beach—technically within Escambia County's jurisdiction though on the island—was assessed $12,500 in cumulative fines last March. The owner, a Georgia-based LLC called Sunset Holdings Group, appealed. The appeal is still pending.

The registration gap

The county requires all short-term rentals to register and pay an annual fee of $250. As of July 1, 2026, the county had 2,847 registered STR properties.

But how many are actually operating?

Henderson's department contracted with a software company called Granicus last year to scrape listing data from Airbnb, Vrbo, and other platforms. The most recent scan, completed in May, identified 4,112 unique rental listings within unincorporated Escambia County.

That's a gap of roughly 1,265 properties—rentals that appear to be operating without registration.

"We send letters," Henderson said. "We send a lot of letters."

The letters inform property owners that they appear to be operating an unpermitted STR and invite them to register within 30 days. (There's that number again.) Some comply. Many don't respond at all. Tracking them down requires cross-referencing platform listings with property appraiser records, which requires staff time the department doesn't have.

Commissioner Bergosh, reached by phone, said he's aware of the gap. "We're doing what we can within our budget. Nobody's getting rich running code enforcement."

The neighbor's dilemma

Linda and Robert Castillo bought their home on Innerarity Point in 2019. It was a retirement plan. Quiet street. Water views. Neighbors they knew by name.

Three of those neighbors have since sold to investors. All three houses are now STRs.

"Every weekend it's someone new," Linda Castillo said, standing in her driveway on a Tuesday afternoon. "They don't know the rules. They don't know us. They're on vacation."

The Castillos have filed 11 complaints with code enforcement since last August. Noise. Parking. A rented pontoon boat that blocked their dock access. They've received form-letter responses confirming each complaint was logged. They've seen one citation posted on the door of the house next door. It was gone by the following weekend.

"What's the point?" Robert Castillo asked. "We call, nothing changes. We're just yelling into the wind."

They've thought about selling. The offers come monthly—postcards and cold calls from investors who see the address and smell opportunity. The Castillos' home, free of rental history, would convert easily.

"Then we're part of the problem," Linda said. "And someone else gets to deal with it."

What would actually work

Thornton, the real estate attorney, said meaningful enforcement requires structural changes the county hasn't been willing to make.

First: Eliminate or shorten the cure period for repeat violations. Santa Rosa County's ordinance, passed in 2024, gives property owners seven days to cure a first offense and no cure period for subsequent violations at the same address. Escambia County's 30-day window applies universally.

Second: Increase fines to a level that changes behavior. Thornton pointed to Walton County, where STR fines start at $1,000 and can reach $5,000 per violation. "It has to hurt," he said. "Otherwise it's just a fee."

Third: Hire more attorneys. Code enforcement can issue citations all day. Without legal staff to prosecute them, the citations are paper.

Henderson said his department has requested two additional positions in the fiscal year 2027 budget—one more code enforcement officer and a dedicated administrative coordinator to track cases through the legal process. The board has not yet voted on the budget.

"We're asking for what we need," Henderson said. "Whether we get it is above my pay grade."

The view from Tallahassee

Florida's legislature has historically preempted local governments from outright banning short-term rentals. A 2011 law grandfathered existing bans but prohibited new ones. A 2014 revision allowed local regulation of "duration and frequency" but not prohibition.

This means Escambia County—and every other Florida county—can restrict how often a property is rented or impose noise and parking rules, but cannot simply say no to STRs altogether. The state's position has been that property rights include the right to rent.

Several bills in the 2026 legislative session would have further restricted local authority, including one that would have capped STR fines at $500 statewide. That bill died in committee after opposition from the Florida League of Cities. But similar proposals return each year.

"Tallahassee ties our hands," Commissioner Litchfield said at a June board meeting. "Then they blame us when people complain."

What happens next

The Board of County Commissioners is scheduled to review STR enforcement data at its August 8 workshop. Henderson will present the first-half complaint numbers and recommend what he's calling "targeted amendments" to the ordinance—likely a shorter cure period and higher base fines.

Whether the board acts is uncertain. Two commissioners face reelection in November. Both represent districts with significant STR concentrations. Property owners vote. So do angry neighbors.

At the house on Perdido Key Drive, the one with the Memorial Day party, a new group arrived last Friday. Seven cars. A stack of pool floats. The listing advertises "sleeps 16."

The Escambia County code sets maximum occupancy at two people per bedroom plus two. The house has four bedrooms. Maximum legal occupancy: 10.

By Saturday night, the code enforcement hotline had logged two more complaints.

Officer Watkins was off for the weekend. She'd be back Monday to write it up.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's summer surge: 800 new student aviators hit the flight line
articles.dek: July marks peak training tempo at the Cradle of Naval Aviation. For instructors and the surrounding community, it means long days, packed airspace and a familiar roar overhead.
brief: NAS Pensacola reaches peak annual training capacity with approximately 800 student naval aviators cycling through primary flight training this month
Training Wing Five instructors are flying six days a week to maintain the accelerated summer schedule, with some logging 30+ flight hours monthly
Local residents near Perdido Key and Warrington report increased noise levels, while base officials cite community notification protocols
articles.body:
At 0615 on a Thursday morning, the sun barely clears the tree line east of Sherman Field. The humidity already hangs thick enough to taste. On the tarmac, a line of orange and white T-6B Texan IIs sits nose to tail, engines ticking as they cool from the first wave of morning flights.

Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Okonkwo walks the line with a clipboard, checking off tail numbers. She's been an instructor pilot with Training Squadron One (VT-1) for two years. By August, she'll have helped certify more than 40 student naval aviators for their next phase of training.

"July is when the machine runs hot," Okonkwo said. "Everyone who started primary in the spring is hitting their check rides. Everyone who just arrived is doing their first familiarization flights. The schedule board looks like a subway map."

NAS Pensacola, the self-proclaimed Cradle of Naval Aviation, reaches its annual peak training tempo every summer. According to Training Wing Five public affairs, approximately 800 student aviators are currently cycling through various stages of primary flight training at the base and its outlying fields. That number represents both Navy and Marine Corps students, plus a smaller contingent of Coast Guard and international partner pilots.

The math of military readiness

The summer surge isn't arbitrary. It's the product of a training pipeline that begins with commissioning ceremonies at Annapolis, Newport and university ROTC programs each May. New ensigns and second lieutenants arrive at Pensacola throughout June, complete ground school and aerospace physiology training, then hit the flight line in earnest by early July.

"We're building next year's fleet aviators right now," said Capt. Marcus Webb, commanding officer of Training Wing Five. "Every student who successfully completes primary here goes on to advanced training in Meridian, Corpus Christi or Kingsville. Eighteen months from now, they're landing on carriers or flying surveillance missions over the Pacific."

Webb declined to provide specific throughput targets, citing operational security. But he acknowledged the pressure to maintain training numbers while the Navy faces persistent pilot shortages across multiple aircraft communities.

Department of Defense data shows the Navy was short approximately 1,300 pilots as of fiscal year 2025, with fighter and electronic attack communities hit hardest. Primary training at Pensacola represents the first bottleneck in addressing that gap.

Long days on the line

For instructor pilots like Okonkwo, the summer surge means six-day weeks and pre-dawn briefs. She typically flies two or three training sorties per day during July, each lasting about 90 minutes. Between flights, she debriefs students, grades maneuvers and enters data into the Naval Aviation Training System database.

"I'll log somewhere between 30 and 35 flight hours this month," she said. "That's on the higher end, but not unusual for summer. You stay hydrated. You stay sharp. You remember that the kid in the front seat is trusting you with their career."

Student naval aviator Ensign David Tran arrived at NAS Pensacola in late May after completing Officer Candidate School in Newport, Rhode Island. He flew his sixth familiarization flight earlier this week, practicing basic air work over Santa Rosa Sound.

"The pace is intense," Tran said. "You're studying every night. Flying every day or every other day. The instructors expect you to show up ready. If you're not prepared, the schedule doesn't care. Someone else takes your slot."

Tran, 24, grew up in Garden Grove, California, and graduated from UCLA with a degree in mechanical engineering. He said he decided to pursue naval aviation after watching Blue Angels demonstrations at the Huntington Beach Air Show as a teenager.

"I knew I wanted to fly. The Navy offered a path," he said. "Now I'm here, and it's harder than I imagined. But it's also exactly what I signed up for."

Noise over Warrington

The summer surge doesn't stay contained to the base. Residents in Warrington, Perdido Key and West Pensacola have reported increased aircraft noise throughout June and into July, with some noting flights as early as 6 a.m. and as late as 9 p.m.

Linda Forsythe has lived on Barrancas Avenue, about two miles from Sherman Field, for 18 years. She said the noise has been "noticeably louder" this summer compared to recent years.

"I understand they have to train. I'm not anti-military," Forsythe said. "But it rattles the windows some days. My dog hides under the bed. I just wish there was more warning about when the heavy days are coming."

NAS Pensacola maintains a community noise complaint line and publishes general training schedules through its public affairs office. But specific daily flight plans are not released in advance due to operational considerations.

Base spokesman Lt. Michael Torres said the installation takes noise concerns seriously and adjusts flight patterns when operationally feasible.

"We try to avoid residential areas during early morning and evening hours when possible," Torres said. "But training requirements have to come first. We appreciate the community's patience and support."

Flight operations at NAS Pensacola are governed by a 1999 Air Installation Compatible Use Zone study, which maps noise contours around the base. Escambia County uses that study to guide zoning decisions, though development has continued in some noise-affected areas over the past two decades.

Economic altitude

The summer surge also ripples through the local economy. Student aviators on training pay spend money in Pensacola. So do their families, many of whom relocate temporarily during the six-month primary training pipeline.

A 2024 economic impact study commissioned by the Florida Defense Support Task Force estimated that NAS Pensacola and its tenant commands contribute approximately $3.2 billion annually to the regional economy. That figure includes military and civilian payroll, contracts and induced spending.

Ryan Tillman owns Tillman's Wings and Wheels, a breakfast spot on Navy Boulevard that caters heavily to military clientele. He said July through September are typically his strongest months.

"Student pilots come in here in their flight suits before their morning briefs," Tillman said. "They're young, they're hungry, they tip pretty good. When training ramps up, my register ramps up."

Tillman estimated that military customers account for roughly 60 percent of his revenue during peak training months.

A tradition renewed

Naval aviation training has operated continuously at NAS Pensacola since 1914, when the Navy established its first aeronautic station on the site of the old Pensacola Navy Yard. The base has trained hundreds of thousands of aviators in the century since, including astronauts, admirals and seven Medal of Honor recipients.

That history hangs over Sherman Field every summer, even if most student aviators are too focused on their next check ride to notice.

Ensign Tran said he visited the National Naval Aviation Museum during his first week at Pensacola. He stood in front of the A-4 Skyhawk that John McCain flew before his capture in Vietnam.

"You realize you're part of something bigger," Tran said. "People have been learning to fly here for over a hundred years. Some of them became heroes. Most of them just did their jobs. Either way, you want to live up to it."

On the flight line, Lt. Cmdr. Okonkwo finished her walkdown and headed back to the squadron building for her next brief. In three hours, she would be airborne over Pensacola Bay, talking a student through a stall recovery for the fourth time that week.

The summer surge continues through August.

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: Downtown's Palafox garage is at capacity by 9 a.m. The city's next move is 18 months away.
articles.dek: A promised 400-space structure won't break ground until 2028. Business owners and city officials are clashing over stopgap solutions as summer tourism peaks.
brief: The Palafox Street parking garage reaches capacity before 9 a.m. most weekdays, forcing downtown workers and visitors to circle blocks or park at the port lot a half-mile away.
A 400-space garage approved in 2024 won't break ground until late 2027 at the earliest, with completion projected for mid-2029.
Business owners are pushing for immediate solutions including validated parking agreements and a shuttle from remote lots, but the city says funding remains a barrier.
articles.body:
The digital sign at the entrance of the Jefferson Street garage flashed "FULL" at 8:47 a.m. on a Tuesday. A silver Camry idled at the gate anyway, its driver staring at the message like it might change. Behind her, three more cars waited. None of them were getting in.

This is downtown Pensacola in July 2026. The city's only public parking structure—a 900-space garage built in 2007—hits capacity before most office workers finish their first coffee. The promised solution, a 400-space garage on the former Brent Building lot at Palafox and Wright streets, exists only as renderings in a city planning document.

Ground won't break until late 2027. Maybe.

The math doesn't work

Downtown Pensacola added roughly 1,200 jobs between 2020 and 2025, according to Florida Department of Economic Opportunity data. The number of public parking spaces in the core district: unchanged.

"We've been running a deficit for years," said Marcus Webb, director of the Downtown Improvement Board. "COVID masked it because nobody was coming downtown. Now they're back, and we're exactly where we were in 2019—except with more restaurants, more offices, more demand."

The Jefferson Street garage serves as the primary parking option for the Escambia County Courthouse, several law firms, and the growing cluster of tech and marketing companies along South Palafox. City data obtained through a public records request shows the garage has reached capacity before 10 a.m. on 73% of weekdays since Memorial Day.

On Saturdays during summer tourist season, it fills by noon.

The garage that isn't

Pensacola City Council approved $18 million in funding for a new parking structure in September 2024. The site—a surface lot at Palafox and Wright where the Brent Building once stood—was supposed to offer relief by late 2026.

That timeline has slipped twice.

First came environmental assessments that revealed contaminated soil from a dry cleaning operation that occupied the site in the 1970s. Remediation added $1.2 million to the project cost and pushed design completion to March 2026. Then steel prices spiked 14% in the first quarter of this year, forcing engineers to revise structural plans.

"We're not going to build something that's over budget before we pour the foundation," said City Administrator Keith Wilkins at a June 24 council workshop. "The responsible thing is to get this right."

Current projections show construction beginning in the fourth quarter of 2027, with the garage opening in mid-2029. Three years from now.

'We can't wait three years'

Jennifer Ramos has owned Palafox Wine Company for eight years. Her shop sits three blocks from the Jefferson Street garage, close enough that she used to tell customers parking was easy. She stopped saying that last spring.

"I've had people call me from the parking garage, frustrated, asking if I can validate somewhere else," Ramos said. "There is nowhere else. They leave. They shop online. They go to Cordova Mall."

A coalition of 34 downtown business owners sent a letter to City Council in May demanding immediate action. Their proposals: negotiate validated parking rates at the Port of Pensacola's surface lot, launch a shuttle service from the Civic Center lot during peak hours, and convert two-hour street parking to four-hour limits.

Council member Allison Patton, whose district includes downtown, called the letter "a wake-up call" at the June 24 workshop. She pushed for a vote on the shuttle proposal at the July 17 meeting.

But City Administrator Wilkins raised concerns about cost. A shuttle running from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays would require two vehicles and four drivers, he said. Annual operating cost: roughly $340,000.

"That's money we don't have in the current budget," Wilkins said. "We'd need to find it somewhere."

The port lot problem

The Port of Pensacola operates a 600-space surface lot at the south end of Palafox, primarily for cruise ship passengers and event parking. On most weekdays, it sits half-empty.

Downtown Improvement Board director Webb has been negotiating with port officials since February to open the lot for daily public parking. The talks have stalled over liability insurance and revenue sharing.

"The port wants a guaranteed minimum payment regardless of how many cars use it," Webb said. "We think usage-based makes more sense. We're not that far apart, but we're not there yet."

Port Authority chairman David Chen declined to comment on the negotiations but said the authority "remains committed to supporting downtown's growth in a way that's consistent with our core mission."

The port lot is a 12-minute walk from the courthouse. For a lawyer hauling case files, or a tourist in Florida's July heat, that might as well be a mile.

What happens next

Council will vote on July 17 whether to allocate $85,000 for a 90-day shuttle pilot program running from the Civic Center lot. If approved, service could begin in early August.

The Downtown Improvement Board is also exploring a partnership with a private parking app that would let drivers reserve street parking spots in advance—technology already deployed in St. Petersburg and Sarasota.

"There's no silver bullet," Webb said. "We need five or six smaller solutions to get us through until that garage opens."

If it opens on schedule. The 2024 approval resolution included language requiring council to reauthorize funding if costs exceed the original $18 million budget by more than 15%. Current estimates put the project at $20.4 million—a 13.3% increase. Another spike in materials costs could trigger a new vote.

Ramos, the wine shop owner, said she's trying to stay patient. She's also looking at real estate in East Hill.

"I love downtown," she said. "I believe in downtown. But my customers have to be able to get here. Right now, that's not a given."

The Jefferson Street garage sign flashed "FULL" again at 8:52 a.m. on Wednesday. Then Thursday. Then Friday.

The Camry driver from Tuesday? She circled the block twice, then headed north on Palafox. Whether she found parking somewhere else, or gave up entirely, is impossible to know.
